title: Chapter X

teacherSummary.text: Miss Bingley flatters Darcy as he writes a letter; Elizabeth and Darcy spar over Bingley's 'humility' and persuadability. Darcy asks Elizabeth to dance a reel; she refuses wittily, and he finds himself 'bewitched.'

vocabulary.definition: To belong or pertain, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom
vocabulary.context: “Will it not be advisable, before we proceed on this subject, to arrange with rather more precision the degree of importance which is to appertain to this request, as well as the degree of intimacy subsisting between the parties?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “appertain”: ap- (Latin ad, "to") + tain (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: You wanted me, I know, to say ‘Yes,’ that you might have the pleasure of despising my taste; but I always delight in overthrowing those kind of schemes, and cheating a person of their premeditated contempt.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overthrow”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “I dare say you believed it; but I am by no means convinced that you would be gone with such celerity.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “celerity”: -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To walk, ride, or sail, from place to place, without any determinate object in view
vocabulary.context: She then ran gaily off, rejoicing as she rambled about, in the hope of being at home again in a day or two.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ramble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To think on, and revolve in the mind, beforehand
vocabulary.context: You wanted me, I know, to say ‘Yes,’ that you might have the pleasure of despising my taste; but I always delight in overthrowing those kind of schemes, and cheating a person of their premeditated contempt.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “premeditate”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To stick fast or cleave, as a glutinous substance does
vocabulary.context: Darcy then consider the rashness of your original intention as atoned for by your obstinacy in adhering to it?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “adhere”: ad- (Latin ad, "to, toward"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The outer part or edge of anything, as of a garment, a garden, etc.; margin
vocabulary.context: And, if I may mention so delicate a subject, endeavour to check that little something, bordering on conceit and impertinence, which your lady possesses.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “border”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Any action toward another which manifests contempt for him
vocabulary.context: Miss Bingley warmly resented the indignity he had received, in an expostulation with her brother for talking such nonsense.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “indignity”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “I am exceedingly gratified,” said Bingley, “by your converting what my friend says into a compliment on the sweetness of my temper.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “convert”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + vert (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Pleasing the mind or senses in a high degree
vocabulary.context: You are charmingly group’d, and appear to uncommon advantage.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “charming”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Letter writing was a central social skill and a sign of character.

significance: Their verbal duels reveal mutual attraction neither admits.
discussionQuestions: Why does Darcy enjoy Elizabeth's refusal rather than resent it?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter X,” how does Austen show wit as courtship? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter X, how does Austen develop the idea of wit as courtship? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter X develops the idea of wit as courtship. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter X (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of wit as courtship. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter X suggests about wit as courtship. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter X to complicate the reader's understanding of wit as courtship. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter X within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of wit as courtship responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter X alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of wit as courtship follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter X and its treatment of wit as courtship. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter X as evidence for a larger claim about wit as courtship in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter X as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of wit as courtship. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: “I dare say you believed it; but I am by no means convinced that you would be gone with such celerity. Your conduct would be quite as dependant on chance as that of any man I know; and if, as you were mounting your horse, a friend were to say, ‘Bingley, you had better stay till next week,’ you would probably do it, you would probably not go—and, at another word, might stay a month.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter X”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “I dare say you believed it; but I am by no means convinced that you would be gone with such celerity. Your conduct would be quite as dependant on chance as that of any man I know; and if, as you were mounting your horse, a friend were to say, ‘Bingley, you had better stay till next week,’ you would probably do it, you would probably not go—and, at another word, might stay a month.”

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Darcy enjoy Elizabeth's refusal rather than resent it? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are appertain, overthrowing, celerity, rambled, premeditated. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““Will it not be advisable, before we proceed on this subject, to arrange with rather more precision the degree of importance which is to appertain to this request, as well as the degree of intimacy subsisting between the parties?”” Webster's says: To belong or pertain, whether by right, nature, appointment, or custom. Now the word history: “appertain”: ap- (Latin ad, "to") + tain (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “overthrow”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “celerity”: -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Letter writing was a central social skill and a sign of character. Why does this chapter matter? Their verbal duels reveal mutual attraction neither admits. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to wit as courtship.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “I dare say you believed it; but I am by no means convinced that you would be gone with such celerity. Your conduct would be quite as dependant on chance as that of any man I know; and if, as you were mounting your horse, a friend were to say, ‘Bingley, you had better stay till next week,’ you would probably do it, you would probably not go—and, at another word, might stay a month.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Irony, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter X,” how does Austen show wit as courtship? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about wit as courtship, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes wit as courtship. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
